issues.subcategory: false significance claim
issues.description: The Discussion section states the meta-analytic effect size for 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' was 'significantly different from zero,' but the Results section explicitly reports p = .065, which does not meet the conventional α = .05 threshold. This is a direct factual error that misrepresents the central conclusion for one of the four key outcomes.
issues.quote: Results: 'The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065.' Discussion: 'However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.'

issues.subcategory: CI/PI confusion in reporting
issues.description: In the Discussion of the Self-Disclosure Safety outcome, the authors label the 95% confidence interval [-.40, -.15] as the prediction interval (PI). The actual PI from the Results section is [-.54, -.03]. These are substantively different ranges with different interpretations: the CI quantifies uncertainty around the mean effect, while the PI quantifies where future single study effects are expected to fall. The mistaken values make the Safety effect appear far more precise and less variable than it actually is.
issues.quote: Results: '95% CI [-.40, -.15], 95% PI [-.54, -.03].' Discussion: 'The 95% PI [-.40, -.15] indicated that future studies would be likely to find such an effect as well.'

issues.subcategory: fail-safe N discrepancy for Connect outcome
issues.description: The Results section reports FSN = 5 for the 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' outcome, but the Discussion section reports FSN = 11 for the same outcome. These are materially different values that lead to different substantive conclusions about result robustness, and only one can be correct.
issues.quote: Results: 'The FSN was 5 studies.' Discussion: 'These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies).'

issues.subcategory: prediction interval discrepancy for Connect outcome
issues.description: The 95% prediction interval reported for the 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' outcome differs between the Results and Discussion sections. Results reports PI [-.09, .26]; Discussion reports PI [-.07, .27]. These are not the same interval. The discrepancy alters whether and by how much the interval extends in the negative direction, affecting interpretation of whether a true negative effect (consistent with the original) remains plausible.
issues.quote: Results: '95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065.' Discussion: 'We believe that it will be unlikely that future studies will find an effect similar to the original, supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero.'

issues.subcategory: fail-safe N discrepancy for Express outcome
issues.description: The Results section reports FSN = 3 for 'Opportunity to Express Self,' but the Discussion section states 'only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant,' implying FSN = 5. These numbers are inconsistent and the interpretation built upon this statistic ('led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect') rests on uncertain data.
issues.quote: Results: 'The FSN was 3 studies.' Discussion: 'The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.'

issues.subcategory: beta vs. r discrepancy for Advantageous outcome
issues.description: The Table 1 note states 'Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient,' which holds only in simple regression with a single predictor. Yet for the Advantageous outcome, the original study's standardized beta is listed as -.300 in Table 1 while Table 3 records the original r as -.33—a discrepancy of .03. In simple regression these must be identical. This suggests either that the original Forest and Wood study used additional covariates (making beta ≠ r), or there is a calculation error. Either way, the note's equivalence claim is wrong for this variable, and affect sizes derived from the original study may be miscalculated.
issues.quote: Table 1: 'Original... β [Advantageous] = -.300'; Table 3: 'Advantageous... Original r = -0.33'; Table 1 Note: 'Beta coefficients are standardized (consistent with the original research). Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.'

issues.subcategory: abstract contradicts meta-analytic result for Express
issues.description: The abstract states 'self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression,' citing individual study CIs as evidence. However, the Results section reports a statistically significant meta-analytic effect (r = .08, p = .021) and a prediction interval [.01, .14] that entirely excludes zero. A significant meta-analytic effect is the primary inferential product of the study and directly contradicts the abstract's categorical claim of no relationship. This inconsistency is likely to mislead readers who rely on the abstract.
issues.quote: Abstract: 'self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero).' Results: 'the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero.'

issues.subcategory: self-contradictory conclusion for Express outcome
issues.description: The Discussion simultaneously states that the prediction interval for Express [.01, .14] does not include zero ('The PI came close to, but did not include, zero so it may be that there is an effect'), while also concluding 'future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.' A PI that excludes zero and a significant meta-analytic p-value (.021) are incompatible with a conclusion of no effect. The discussion arrives at two opposing conclusions within the same paragraph.
issues.quote: 'The PI came close to, but did not include, zero so it may be that there is an effect, but small enough to be difficult to detect. The FSN analysis...led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.'

issues.subcategory: publication bias claim is directionally inverted for Express
issues.description: The authors claim that the pattern for Express (replication effect sizes smaller than the original) indicates 'the presence of publication bias in the original study.' However, publication bias would inflate published effects upward. For Express, the original study reported a non-significant finding (p = .181) while the replications found a small but significant positive effect (r = .08). If anything, this pattern suggests the original was underpowered to detect a small true effect, not that it was inflated by publication bias. The claim is conceptually backwards for this specific outcome.
issues.quote: 'the summary effect size was about half of the original's effect size, and the PI [.01, .14] showed that 95% of future studies would find an effect size smaller than the original study's, all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study.'

issues.subcategory: measurement scale non-equivalence across studies
issues.description: Two of the seven replication studies (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point response scale for the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, while the remaining five studies and the original used a four-point scale. Response scale format affects item means, variances, and potentially factor structure. No measurement invariance tests were conducted to verify that scores are comparable across scale formats before pooling effect sizes in the meta-analysis. This introduces a confound between institution and scale format, making it impossible to attribute observed effect size heterogeneity to substantive vs. methodological sources.
issues.quote: 'most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale.'

issues.subcategory: item wording alteration in IIT-Sp16
issues.description: One study (IIT-Sp16) modified the wording of four of the ten Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale items while also using a non-standard five-point response scale. This study is thus doubly non-equivalent to the original instrument. Modified item wording can shift item difficulty, endorsement rates, and factor loadings. The simultaneous alteration of both wording and scale format means any observed differences for IIT-Sp16 cannot be attributed to a single source. This compromises the 'direct replication' designation for this study.
issues.quote: 'one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., 'At times I think I am no good at all' vs. 'I think I am no good at all')'

issues.subcategory: group vs. individual administration confound
issues.description: Participants in the SAU replication completed questionnaires in groups of two to six participants, while all other lab-based replications administered questionnaires individually. Social presence during questionnaire completion is particularly problematic for a study measuring self-disclosure attitudes and self-esteem, as participants may adjust their self-reports due to social desirability or awareness of others' responses. This procedural deviation is uncontrolled and not included in any moderation analysis.
issues.quote: 'Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.'

issues.subcategory: composite score calculation inconsistency
issues.description: Most replication studies mean-averaged scale items to create composite scores, but the Gordon College replication appears to have summed items instead, based on reported means. Item averaging and item summing differ by a factor equal to the number of items, and while standardized regression betas are scale-invariant, summed scores will have different variances that could affect standard errors and, under listwise deletion or missing data conditions, produce different effective sample sizes per analysis. More critically, this inconsistency reveals a lack of standardized data preparation protocols across sites.
issues.quote: 'Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed.'

issues.subcategory: missing data handling unknown for most studies
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that most replication teams did not post analysis scripts and that procedures for handling missing data are therefore unknown. Missing data can be handled by listwise deletion, pairwise deletion, mean imputation, or model-based imputation, each producing different effective sample sizes and potentially different effect estimates. Without knowing how each team treated missing data, it is impossible to evaluate whether the pooled effect sizes are comparable across studies or to replicate the individual study analyses.
issues.quote: 'Contributors did not always post analysis scripts, so procedures to account for missing data are not known for all studies.'

issues.subcategory: causal language from cross-sectional correlational data
issues.description: The study collected self-esteem and Facebook perception measures at a single time point in a cross-sectional survey design, yet the Discussion frames findings in causal language. Regression coefficients from observational data do not establish causal direction, and numerous third variables (e.g., social anxiety, extraversion, frequency of Facebook use) could explain the observed associations without any causal role for self-esteem.
issues.quote: 'We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions, and that the size of this effect is considerable.'

issues.subcategory: original study excluded from meta-analysis without justification
issues.description: The meta-analysis synthesizes only the seven replication studies and explicitly excludes the original Forest and Wood (2012) study. Including the original in a combined meta-analysis is standard practice when estimating a true underlying effect and is explicitly recommended as one of Anderson & Maxwell's (2016) goals cited in this paper (Goal 4). No rationale is given for excluding it. Inclusion would shift summary estimates (particularly for Safety and Advantageous where the original effect is the largest single data point) and affect precision of the pooled estimates.
issues.quote: 'This meta-analysis synthesized seven direct pre-registered replications of Forest and Wood (2012) Study 1 that were part of the CREP project.' [No mention of including the original study in the meta-analysis or justification for its exclusion.]

issues.subcategory: original Express beta not available, yet effect size r reported
issues.description: The original Forest and Wood (2012) study did not report a standardized beta coefficient for the 'Opportunity to Express Self' outcome. Table 3 nonetheless reports an original r = .15. It is unclear how this value was derived—presumably back-calculated from the reported p-value (.181) and degrees of freedom—but the derivation method is not described. Readers cannot verify this value, and back-calculation from p introduces rounding error. The table note only states the beta was not available; it does not explain how r = .15 was obtained.
issues.quote: Table 1 Note: '* The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable.' Table 3: 'Express... Original r = 0.15'

issues.subcategory: missing analysis scripts and item-level data
issues.description: Several critical analysis details are unverifiable because most research teams did not post analysis scripts and item-level data were not always stored. This makes it impossible to independently verify exclusion criteria, scale construction, outlier handling, and data transformations for the majority of the contributing studies—undermining the open-science ethos the project champions and making replication of the meta-analysis itself impossible for several constituent datasets.
issues.quote: 'individual item-level data were not always stored... Contributors did not always post analysis scripts, so procedures to account for missing data are not known for all studies.'

issues.subcategory: two IIT samples not fully independent
issues.description: Two of the seven replication studies (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) were conducted at the same institution (Illinois Institute of Technology) by the same faculty mentor (Legate, et al.) in consecutive semesters. Non-independence between studies violates the random-effects meta-analytic assumption that studies are drawn from independent populations. Participants from the same institution and same research group are likely subject to shared local culture, recruitment pools, and procedural micro-norms. This inflates the effective number of independent replications and may bias heterogeneity estimates. No correction (e.g., three-level meta-analysis) is applied.
issues.quote: 'IIT-Sp16 | Legate, et al.... IIT-Sp17 | Legate, et al.' [Both from Illinois Institute of Technology, same mentor team, consecutive semesters.]

issues.subcategory: mixed online and in-person administration without randomization
issues.description: Administration mode varied across and within studies (three lab-only, two online-only, two hybrid) with no control or randomization. Mode of administration can affect response rates, item interpretation, social desirability, and careless responding differently. Particularly for self-esteem and self-disclosure measures, anonymous online completion may elicit more candid responding than lab settings. This systematic variation is not included in moderator analyses and cannot be disentangled from institution-level variation.
issues.quote: 'As the original research did not specify whether participants completed questionnaires in a lab or online, researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods).'

issues.subcategory: undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom in meta-analysis decisions
issues.description: Several consequential analytic choices are made without pre-registration or justification at the meta-analysis level: (1) choice of REML over DL estimator; (2) use of effect size r rather than d or z; (3) exclusion of the original study from pooling; (4) use of Rosenberg (2005) FSN rather than more robust publication bias methods (e.g., Egger's test, PET-PEESE, trim-and-fill); and (5) the decision to report prediction intervals alongside CIs. Individual study pre-registrations cover data collection but not the subsequent meta-analytic synthesis protocol. The manuscript states pre-registration occurred at each study's OSF page, but no meta-analysis-level pre-registration is referenced.
issues.quote: 'This manuscript qualifies for a Preregistration badge; the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study's OSF page.' [No mention of a meta-analysis-level pre-registration covering the synthesis decisions.]

issues.subcategory: heterogeneity statistics unreliable for k=7 but used interpretively
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that 'heterogeneity measures are known to be biased for meta-analysis involving small numbers of studies' and state they are 'reluctant to draw conclusive inferences from the heterogeneity statistics.' However, they nonetheless report and interpret Q, I², and τ² throughout the Results section, drawing substantive conclusions (e.g., 'The between-study variance in the replication studies did not appear to be heterogeneous' and 'The between-study variance showed some evidence of heterogeneity'). The Q test is severely underpowered with k=7 studies, making both low and high I² values uninterpretable. Reporting conclusions about heterogeneity from these statistics contradicts the authors' own caveat.
issues.quote: 'The between-study variance in the replication studies did not appear to be heterogenous, Q(df = 6) = 4.75, p = .576; T2 = 0, 95% CI [0, .03]; I2 = 0%...' and later: 'heterogeneity measures are known to be biased for meta-analysis involving small numbers of studies... we are reluctant to draw conclusive inferences from the heterogeneity statistics.'

issues.subcategory: fail-safe N methodology is widely criticized but used as primary robustness evidence
issues.description: The Rosenthal fail-safe N (FSN) is the sole publication-bias and robustness analysis conducted. The FSN has been extensively criticized because it assumes missing studies have zero effect (unrealistic), does not account for study quality, and produces artificially large numbers for even modest meta-analyses. More appropriate modern methods—Egger's regression test, trim-and-fill, or PET-PEESE—are not used. With only seven studies the power for any bias test is low, but the FSN particularly is not suited to small-k scenarios. Conclusions such as 'the findings were relatively stable' based solely on FSN are not well-supported.
issues.quote: 'Finally, we conducted a fail-safe number (FSN) analysis (Rosenberg, 2005) using the fsn function. The FSN analysis was intended to identify the number of non-significant, unreported studies required to add to the meta-analysis to reduce a significant meta-analytic result to non-significance.' [No alternative publication bias test is conducted.]

issues.subcategory: exclusive reliance on U.S. undergraduate convenience samples
issues.description: All seven replication samples consist exclusively of U.S. undergraduate students at five institutions. The abstract and Discussion draw conclusions about Facebook users generally (e.g., 'individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook'), yet Facebook's user base spans all age groups and dozens of national cultures. The study does not adequately flag this as a generalizability constraint. The comparison to Eşkisu et al.'s Turkish sample acknowledges cultural variation but is framed as an anomaly rather than evidence that findings may not generalize beyond the sampled population.
issues.quote: 'We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions, and that the size of this effect is considerable.'

issues.subcategory: Facebook perceptions scale not validated and created by original authors
issues.description: The Facebook perceptions measure was created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012) and its psychometric properties (factor structure, discriminant validity, convergent validity) are not reported beyond internal consistency (Cronbach's α). The items assess four distinct constructs (expression, connection, safety, advantages), but no confirmatory factor analysis is cited to justify treating them as separable subscales. Two of the subscales (safety: 9 items; advantages: 10 items) overlap substantially in apparent content (both address disclosure on Facebook vs. FTF), yet their discriminant validity is not established.
issues.quote: 'Three items each assessed the degree to which participants believed Facebook enabled them to express themselves and to connect with others. Perceived safety of self-disclosure on Facebook compared to in person interactions was measured with nine items. Ten more items assessed perceived advantages of disclosing on Facebook versus FTF.'

issues.subcategory: Connect direction characterization ambiguous in abstract
issues.description: The abstract states 'there was no evidence for self-esteem predicting perceived opportunities for connection with others on Facebook (six of the seven replication effect size CIs contained zero).' However, the Results and Discussion reveal that six of seven replication effects were in the OPPOSITE direction from the original (positive rather than negative). Characterizing this as 'no evidence' obscures a more specific and informative finding: the replications systematically show a directional reversal relative to the original, not a null replication. A positive pooled effect (r = .09) in the opposite direction to the original (r = -.22) represents a qualitatively different outcome than mere non-replication.
issues.quote: Abstract: 'there was no evidence for self-esteem predicting perceived opportunities for connection with others on Facebook (six of the seven replication effect size CIs contained zero).' Results: 'In all but one of the replications, the direction of the effect was opposite of the original study.'

issues.subcategory: minimum sample size set to original study's underpowered N
issues.description: The CREP protocol set the minimum replication sample size equal to the original study's N = 80. Given that original study effect sizes ranged from r = -.22 to r = -.31, power calculations for detecting the smallest of these effects (r ≈ .22) at α = .05 requires approximately N = 160 for 80% power. The N = 80 threshold provides roughly 50% power for the smallest original effect. Five of the seven replication studies collected between 80 and 116 participants, meaning most studies were substantially underpowered, making non-replication of smaller effects uninterpretable (failed replication vs. insufficient power).
issues.quote: 'the CREP team specified the minimum sample size required for the replication; this size was generally set at the original study's sample size... collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (80 for the present study as this was the sample size in the original study)'

issues.subcategory: mischaracterization of p-value distribution literature
issues.description: The authors cite Masicampo & Lalande (2012) and Lakens & Evers (2014) to argue that the original study's p = .050 for the Connect outcome is 'relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one.' This misrepresents the cited literature. Masicampo & Lalande found that p-values just below .05 (e.g., .04–.049) are overrepresented relative to expectation under chance, suggesting p-hacking—not that such values are diagnostic of a true null. A p = .050 at the precise boundary is not addressed by that analysis. The inferential leap from 'suspicious p-value' to 'likely true null' is not supported by the cited work.
issues.quote: 'It is worth noting that the original study obtained a p-value of .05, and p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one (Lakens & Evers, 2014; Masicampo & Lelande, 2012).'
